newsitem.title: FRANCE: Euro currency may smooth French cohabitation.
newsitem.headline: Euro currency may smooth French cohabitation.

text.p: After their first tiff, President Jacques Chirac and Prime Minister Lionel Jospin are likely to keep their forced marriage off the rocks in the interest of a single European currency, analysts said on Thursday.

Socialist Jospin criticised conservative Chirac at a cabinet meeting on Wednesday for breaking a six-week truce in their uneasy "cohabitation" power-sharing by criticising government policies ranging from immigration to nuclear power.
Many analysts dismissed the clash as inevitable skirmishing at the start of France's third bout of cohabitation in 11 years. Jospin swept to power in an upset June 1 parliamentary election.
"There's nothing unusual in it...the president is free to speak and the prime minister is free to act," said Jacques Attali, former chief adviser to the late Socialist president Francois Mitterrand.

Mitterrand shared power in 1986-88 with Chirac as prime minister, in a relationship that got off to a far more acerbic start, and in 1993-95 in a so-called "velvet cohabitation" with conservative premier Edouard Balladur.
"It's pretty normal at the start of this experience for each to clearly define his intentions, his powers and the way in which he plans to exercise them," Balladur told Europe 1 radio.
"Cohabitation is not a bed of roses," he added.
Attali told Reuters: "I'm convinced that cohabitation will last five years and will be effective as it should allow the two sides to work together for European integration and a single currency.
"This is the major historic step facing France, and they agree on it," he said. Neither Chirac nor Jospin would want to be blamed for causing a crisis that could jeopardise that goal.

Political commentator Alain Duhamel also predicted that the two would be condemned to cooperate during the early years of cohabitation to secure the euro. Chirac's term and that of the new parliament both run to 2002.

After criticising Jospin, Chirac sounded a more conciliatory note on Thursday, saying in Brussels that a European Union jobs summit was of vital importance to France. Jospin has said the EU should give more stress to jobs as it moves towards the euro.

Chirac triggered the spat on Monday in a Bastille Day address, saying the constitution gave him "the last word" on a broad range of domestic policy issues. Jospin rebuffed him at Wednesday's cabinet meeting, citing the 1958 constitution.
Yet the constitution is vague, saying the government "determines and conducts the nation's policy" while giving the president a pre-eminent role in foreign affairs.

The left-wing daily Liberation said the two could soon clash over budget deficit curbs needed to help France qualify for the euro. Chirac has constitutional responsibility for ensuring respect of treaties and could claim a say in fixing the budget.

Eleven years to the day before Chirac's broadside, Mitterrand triggered a clash with then-prime minister Chirac by announcing he was refusing to sign decrees speeding up privatisation and scrapping administrative controls on layoffs.
Chirac backed down in 1986, pushing through legislation by the longer route through parliament.
Chirac also needs to speak out to assert himself as leader of the right-wing after he called the election, wrongly gambling that his centre-right allies would be re-elected.

Mitterrand's cohabitation with Balladur was less abrasive than the Mitterrand-Chirac tandem partly because Mitterrand was not running for president in 1995 after two terms. Mitterrand beat Chirac in the 1988 presidential race.
If it lasts, cohabitation could turn sour as both Chirac, 64, and Jospin, 59, may seek election for president in 2002.
Balladur once remarked that rival prime ministers and presidents had to avoid sparking clashes, fearing a backlash from voters. "The first one to draw is a dead man," he said.
